# Mountain composite in New Zealand

This tutorial combines a month of acquisitions around Aoraki / Mount Cook into
one backscatter composite. In steep terrain, a single acquisition sees some
slopes poorly, so combining several viewing directions helps most there.


## Process and compose

The search covers January 2022 for every burst overlapping a small area around
the mountain. Each 10 km grid square that the area touches lies in UTM zone
59 South (EPSG:32759), so the bursts are processed into RTC backscatter in that
zone, `squares[0].crs`, at 20 m, the pixel size of the composite. Each square
is then composed; see [Compositing](compositing.qmd) for the methods used.

::: {#ea223558 .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from freezebase.mgrs import MGRSGrid
from shapely.geometry import box
from s1bursts import BurstCatalog, BurstProcessor, FileManager, ResolutionWeighter, RTCConfig, SearchQuery, TimeRange
from s1bursts.product import Layer

fm = FileManager("data/mountain")
catalog = BurstCatalog(fm)
window = TimeRange("2022-01-01", "2022-01-31")
aoi = box(170.12, -43.62, 170.16, -43.58)
squares = list(MGRSGrid(aoi, resolution=20))
bursts = catalog.search(SearchQuery(time_range=window, intersects=aoi, polarization="VV"))
print(f"{len(bursts)} acquisitions from {bursts.df.rel_orbit_number.nunique()} orbits")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
4 acquisitions from 2 orbits
```
:::
:::


::: {#43ca7ada .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
catalog.download(bursts).raise_on_failure()
processor = BurstProcessor(fm)
rtc = processor.create_backscatter(
    bursts, crs=squares[0].crs, config=RTCConfig(grid_spacing=20),
).raise_on_failure()
```
:::


::: {#5b67dac3 .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
weighter = ResolutionWeighter(fm)
composites = [
    weighter.compose_rtc_lrw(rtc.products, square, write_qa=True, time_range=window)
    for square in squares
]
print(f"{len(composites)} grid squares composed")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
4 grid squares composed
```
:::
:::


## Inspect the composite and its quality layers

The figure joins the four grid squares into one mosaic, for the composite and
for each of its two quality layers. The triangle marks the summit of Aoraki /
Mount Cook. The colour scales are clipped for display; the files keep the full
range of values.

::: {#025c3808 .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from pyproj import Transformer
from rasterio.merge import merge


def mosaic(composites, layer):
    """Join the grid squares of one layer; return the data and its extent in km."""
    data, transform = merge([fm.get_product_path(c, layer) for c in composites])
    rows, cols = data.shape[1:]
    left, top = transform.c, transform.f
    extent = [left, left + transform.a * cols, top + transform.e * rows, top]
    return data[0].astype("float32"), [v / 1000 for v in extent]


summit = Transformer.from_crs("EPSG:4326", "EPSG:32759", always_xy=True).transform(170.1418, -43.5950)
layers = [
    (Layer.MEASUREMENT, "Gamma-0 (dB)", "gray", (-25, 0)),
    (Layer.QA_NUM, "Contributing acquisitions", "viridis", (0, len(bursts))),
    (Layer.QA_CQM, "CQM (dB)", "viridis", (-10, 10)),
]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 4.2), sharey=True, layout="constrained")
for ax, (layer, label, cmap, limits) in zip(axes, layers):
    data, extent = mosaic(composites, layer)
    if label.endswith("(dB)"):
        data = 10 * np.log10(data)
    else:
        data[data == 0] = np.nan  # 0 marks pixels without data in QA-NUM
    image = ax.imshow(data, extent=extent, cmap=cmap, vmin=limits[0], vmax=limits[1])
    ax.plot(summit[0] / 1000, summit[1] / 1000, "^", color="tab:red", markersize=8)
    ax.set(title=label, xlabel="Easting (km)")
    fig.colorbar(image, ax=ax, shrink=0.8)
axes[0].set_ylabel("Northing (km)")
plt.show()
```

## Interpret the result

The composite fills in where single acquisitions fail. In steep terrain, each
acquisition sees some slopes poorly: those facing the satellite are squeezed
into a few pixels, and those facing away can fall into shadow. Local
resolution weighting takes each pixel mostly from the acquisitions that see it
best.

The two quality layers show how well that worked. `QA-NUM`, in the middle,
counts the acquisitions that contributed to each pixel; it steps from two to
four where the bursts of the two orbits overlap, and the white gaps are ground
that no acquisition saw. `QA-CQM`, on the right, is high where the combined
acquisitions resolve the ground finely and low on the steep slopes that all of
them see poorly. [Local resolution weighting](resolution-weighting.qmd)
explains both layers.

Both orbits in this example are descending. Adding ascending orbits, which view
the mountains from the other side, would improve the poorly seen slopes most.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Run details

Run on 02 November 2026 with s1bursts 0.7.1.dev33+g6d2f37539 and ESA SNAP 13.0.0. Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data (2022).
